tag: Earnings season meets the Fed calendar
title: I checked 421,885 earnings releases. Fed day changes nothing.
sub: Every US earnings 8-K since 2005, timed to the second, tested against the FOMC, CPI and jobs calendar.
The Fed meets eight times a year, and every one of those meetings lands in earnings season. One release in seven trades for the first time in the same session as CPI, the jobs report or the Fed.

tag: Announcements per day, 2005–2025 · orange dots are FOMC days
title: Two bands of earnings a year. The Fed sits in the darker one.
EDGAR stamps every filing to the second. That's how I split the sessions.
sub: A 06:46 filing on a CPI day competes with the 08:30 print. A 16:30 filing on Fed day competes with nothing.

title: What I actually did
steps: Pulled every 8-K with Item 2.02 from EDGAR and took the time of day from the acceptance stamp.
Called a release crowded if it first traded in the same session as CPI, payrolls or the FOMC statement.
Measured the surprise two ways: first-filed GAAP EPS against last year, and the two-day market move.
Measured drift over 60 days against FF5 plus momentum, with firm and quarter fixed effects and errors clustered by firm and day.
Wrote the thresholds down first. Held out 2016–2025 and ran it once.

title: Earnings released on crowded days drift the same as any other
sub: Top minus bottom surprise decile after the two-day reaction. 26,531 extreme events, 2005–2025.

title: My first sample found less drift on Fed days. The holdout killed it.
sub: Blue: the primary test in each sample. Grey: by release type. Nothing survives both periods.

title: I redrew the macro calendar at random 1,000 times. Same answer.
sub: 30% of random calendars produce a bigger coefficient than the real one did.

title: Illiquid stocks drift 3.6x more. Fed day still doesn't matter.
sub: The textbook effect is there. Split by Corwin-Schultz spread, the crowded-session effect is flat in all three groups.

title: Firms don't hide bad quarters behind the Fed
sub: Same share of weak quarters on crowded and quiet sessions in both samples (t −0.01 and 1.2).

tag: What firms do shift · exploratory, not pre-registered
title: Bad news doesn't move the date. It moves the filing.
sub: Weak quarters are 1 pp more likely to file the 8-K late (t 5.8, n 177,209) and more likely to land Friday after the close.

title: Drift was over 4 pp in 2007, almost 4 in 2024, and zero in 2020
sub: 60-day drift by year, top vs bottom decile, with 95% bands. My test runs inside this.

title: I wouldn't trade either of these
sub: Quiet-session book: 1.2 bp a day, t 1.9, 237 names. Crowded: 0.6 bp, t 0.4, 50 names. Both lose after spreads.

title: Where I'd push back on myself
items: Prices come from Yahoo Finance, so most delisted firms are missing. Their crowded share was 14.6% against 15.9% for survivors.
GAAP EPS against last year isn't the consensus number analysts actually trade.
The holdout standard error is 0.66 pp, so an effect under about 1.3 pp, top versus bottom decile, could still be there.
The slides marked exploratory weren't pre-registered. I dropped 737 tickers that moved more than 100% in a day.

title: I think the market reads earnings fine on Fed day.
sub: The market prices an earnings release on a CPI, jobs or FOMC session about as fully as on a quiet one, and firms don't use those days to bury weak quarters. What they delay is the 8-K itself. What would change my mind: a consensus-based surprise, or prices for the delisted firms, showing a gap this data can't see.
